title: Legal Alcohol Limit to Drive: BAC Limits by State and Country
excerpt: The legal blood alcohol limit to drive is 0.08% in most US states (0.05% in Utah). Here's how limits work for commercial and under-21 drivers, other countries, how many drinks it takes, and why the legal limit isn't a safe limit.
metaDescription: The legal alcohol limit to drive is 0.08% BAC in most US states, 0.05% in Utah. Limits by country, how many drinks it takes, and why no number is safe.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The answer first:** in the United States, the legal blood alcohol limit for drivers 21 and over is **0.08% BAC** in every state except Utah, where it is **0.05%**. Commercial drivers face a stricter **0.04%** limit, and drivers under 21 are held to "zero tolerance" limits of 0.00% to 0.02%, depending on the state. Many other countries draw the line lower, most often at 0.05%.

**The part that matters more:** the legal limit is not a safe limit. Driving skills start to slip well below 0.08%, you can be arrested and convicted for impaired driving under the limit, and there is no reliable way to count drinks and know you're under it. The only number that guarantees you're legal and unimpaired is zero. If you've been drinking, the safe plan is to not drive: get a ride, take a taxi or rideshare, or stay put.

> **This is general information, not legal or medical advice.** Drunk-driving laws change and vary by state and country, and the details (penalties, how tests work, what counts as impairment) depend on where you are. For your specific situation, check your state's DMV or highway safety office, or talk to a lawyer. **If someone has been drinking heavily and is confused, vomiting while drowsy, breathing slowly or irregularly, or can't be woken, call 911.** Those are signs of alcohol poisoning, which is a medical emergency.

## What Does BAC Actually Measure?

BAC stands for **blood alcohol concentration** (also called blood alcohol content). It's the amount of alcohol in your blood, written as a percentage. A BAC of 0.08% means there are 0.08 grams of alcohol in every 100 milliliters of blood. Put another way, about one part alcohol for every 1,250 parts blood.

That sounds tiny, and it is. But alcohol acts directly on your brain, and even small concentrations change how you think, see, and react. For a full walk-through of what each level feels like, see our guide on [what BAC is and what each level feels like](/never-hungover/what-is-bac).

Police usually measure it in one of two ways:

- **A breath test.** A breathalyzer measures alcohol in the air from deep in your lungs and converts it to an estimated blood level. Many countries write their legal limits directly in breath units (more on that below).
- **A blood test.** A sample taken at a hospital or police station gives a direct reading. It's often used when a breath test isn't possible or when the reading is disputed.

Some states also allow urine testing, but breath and blood are the standard.

## The Legal BAC Limit in the United States

Here is how the US limits break down. These are general figures. Your state's exact rules, and the penalties attached, can differ.

| Driver | Legal BAC limit |
|---|---|
| Adults 21+ (49 states and DC) | 0.08% |
| Adults 21+ in Utah | 0.05% |
| Commercial drivers (CDL holders in a commercial vehicle) | 0.04% |
| Drivers under 21 | 0.00% to 0.02% ("zero tolerance," varies by state) |

### Why 0.08% in most states

For decades, many states set their limit at 0.10%. Federal law in 2000 tied a portion of highway funding to states adopting 0.08%, and by the mid-2000s every state had made the switch. The 0.08% figure is a policy choice. It reflects the level at which impairment and crash risk are clearly elevated for most people, not the point where impairment begins.

### Utah's 0.05% limit

Utah became the first US state to lower its limit to 0.05%, with the change taking effect at the end of 2018. That put it in line with much of Europe and Australia. In Utah, a reading of 0.05% or higher is enough on its own for a DUI charge.

### Commercial drivers: 0.04%

Federal rules set a 0.04% limit for anyone driving a commercial motor vehicle, such as a semi-truck or a bus, under a commercial driver's license. Commercial drivers who refuse a test or are caught over the limit can lose their CDL, which for many means losing their job. Some employers and federal rules also impose stricter "no alcohol within a set number of hours before duty" requirements on top of the BAC limit.

### Under 21: zero tolerance

Because it's illegal for people under 21 to buy or drink alcohol in the US, every state has a "zero tolerance" law for young drivers. Federal highway funding rules from the mid-1990s pushed states to set a limit of 0.02% or lower for drivers under 21. Some states use 0.02%, some use 0.01%, and some use 0.00%. The small margin above zero in some states exists mainly to allow for testing error and trace amounts from things like mouthwash, not to permit a drink.

In practice, if you're under 21, assume any drinking at all before driving puts your license at risk.

## Legal Driving Limits in Other Countries

Many countries set the line lower than the US. Laws change, so treat this as a general guide and check local rules before you drive abroad.

| Country or region | General limit for most adult drivers |
|---|---|
| United States | 0.08% (Utah 0.05%) |
| Canada | 0.08% criminal limit; most provinces apply roadside penalties from 0.05% |
| England and Wales | 0.08% (80 mg per 100 ml of blood) |
| Scotland | 0.05% (50 mg per 100 ml of blood) |
| Ireland | 0.05%, with a lower limit for learner, novice, and professional drivers |
| Australia | 0.05% nationwide, with zero for learner and probationary drivers |
| New Zealand | 0.05% for drivers 20 and over; zero for drivers under 20 |
| Most of the European Union | 0.05%, with lower limits for new and professional drivers in many countries |
| Japan | 0.03% |
| Sweden and Norway | 0.02% |
| Some countries (for example, Czech Republic and Hungary) | Effectively zero |

A few points worth knowing:

- **Canada has two layers.** Driving at 0.08% or above is a criminal offense under federal law. Most provinces also have administrative penalties, such as an immediate roadside license suspension and vehicle impound, that kick in at 0.05%. So in much of Canada, 0.05% can cost you your license for days even if it isn't a crime.
- **The UK isn't uniform.** Scotland lowered its limit to 0.05% in 2014. England and Wales still use 0.08%. If you're driving across the border, the stricter rule applies the moment you cross.
- **New drivers often face tighter rules.** Many countries, including Australia, New Zealand, and much of Europe, set zero or near-zero limits for learners, newly licensed drivers, and professional drivers.

### Breath limits versus blood limits

Outside the US, you'll often see limits written in breath units, such as "35 micrograms per 100 ml of breath" in England and Wales or "22 micrograms" in Scotland. These are simply the breath-test equivalents of the blood limits in the table. You don't need to convert them. If you're driving in another country, the easiest rule is the same everywhere: don't drink and drive.

## How Many Drinks Get You to 0.08%?

This is the question most people really want answered, and the honest answer is that **nobody can tell you a safe number of drinks.** Charts that say "a 160-pound man can have four beers" are rough averages. They can be badly wrong for you on a given night.

That said, it helps to understand the general ballpark and why it varies so much.

### A standard drink

In the US, one standard drink contains about 14 grams of pure alcohol. That's roughly:

- 12 ounces of regular beer (around 5% alcohol)
- 5 ounces of wine (around 12% alcohol)
- 1.5 ounces of 80-proof liquor (40% alcohol)

Many real-world drinks are bigger than this. A craft IPA can be 7% to 9% alcohol and come in a 16-ounce can, which is closer to two or even three standard drinks. A generous restaurant pour of wine or a mixed drink with a double shot can also count as two.

### Rough estimates

You will see charts online that list a number of drinks for a given body weight. We don't repeat them here on purpose. They are averages built on assumptions about pour size, food, and timing that rarely match a real night, and smaller people and anyone drinking on an empty stomach can reach the limit on fewer drinks than any chart suggests. The same person can land at very different BAC levels on different nights. If you plan to drive, the only number that works is zero.

### What changes your BAC

Several things affect how high your BAC climbs from the same amount of alcohol:

- **Body weight and composition.** Alcohol spreads through the water in your body. Smaller people, and people with a higher proportion of body fat, have less water to dilute it, so their BAC rises higher.
- **Sex.** On average, women reach a higher BAC than men from the same amount of alcohol, partly because of differences in body water and partly because of differences in how alcohol is processed in the stomach.
- **Food.** Eating before or while drinking slows how fast alcohol reaches your bloodstream and can lower your peak BAC. Drinking on an empty stomach does the opposite.
- **How fast you drink.** Your liver can only clear alcohol at a fairly fixed rate. Drinking quickly lets alcohol pile up faster than it's removed.
- **Drink strength and size.** A "drink" at a bar or at home is often more than a standard drink.
- **Medications.** Some medicines affect how you process alcohol or add their own sedating effects, which can make you more impaired at the same BAC.

### Why online calculators and phone apps can mislead you

BAC calculators use a formula (usually a version of the Widmark formula) that plugs in your weight, sex, drinks, and time. They give a reasonable estimate on paper. They can't account for how much you actually poured, what you ate, how your body is handling alcohol that night, or the fact that BAC can still be rising after your last drink. Consumer breathalyzers are better than guessing, but cheaper models can be inaccurate, and police equipment is calibrated differently. None of these tools should be the reason you decide to drive.

## Can You Get a DUI Below 0.08%?

Yes. This surprises a lot of people, but it's one of the most important things to understand about drunk-driving laws.

Most US states have two separate ways to charge someone:

1. **"Per se" DUI.** If your BAC is at or above the legal limit, that alone is the offense. Prosecutors don't need to show you were driving badly.
2. **Impaired driving.** If an officer believes alcohol has impaired your ability to drive safely, you can be charged even if your BAC is under the limit. Evidence can include how you were driving, your behavior, field sobriety tests, and the BAC reading itself.

So a reading of 0.06% doesn't mean you're in the clear. If you were weaving, ran a light, or failed field sobriety tests, you can still be charged and convicted. This is also why mixing alcohol with other substances, including some prescription medicines and cannabis, can get you into trouble at a low BAC.

### Implied consent

Most states have "implied consent" laws. By driving on public roads, you're considered to have agreed to a breath or blood test if lawfully arrested for suspected drunk driving. Refusing usually brings its own penalties, often an automatic license suspension, separate from any DUI charge. The rules differ by state, so if this is relevant to you, a lawyer in your state is the right person to ask.

## The Legal Limit Isn't a Safe Limit

The 0.08% line is a legal threshold, not a measure of when you become unsafe. Research on alcohol and driving consistently shows that impairment starts at much lower levels.

The US National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) describes the general pattern this way:

- **Around 0.02%:** some loss of judgment, a slight decline in visual function, and a reduced ability to do two things at once. That's after roughly one to two drinks for many people.
- **Around 0.05%:** reduced coordination, a lowered ability to track moving objects, difficulty steering, and slower responses to emergencies.
- **Around 0.08%:** poor muscle coordination, worse speed control, impaired perception, and reduced ability to process information and react.

Crash risk rises as BAC rises, and the climb gets steeper at higher levels. That pattern has been documented since large studies in the 1960s and has been confirmed many times since. It's also one reason so many countries, and now Utah, have moved to 0.05%.

There's another catch. Alcohol impairs judgment before it noticeably impairs how you feel. People at 0.05% to 0.08% often feel "fine" or "barely buzzed," which is exactly the state where they're most likely to talk themselves into driving. Feeling okay is not evidence that you are okay.

## How Long After Drinking Can You Drive?

There's no reliable countdown, and we won't give you one. Your liver clears alcohol at its own pace, which varies from person to person and night to night, and you can't feel or calculate exactly where your BAC is. **When in doubt, don't drive.** Plan a ride, a designated driver, or a place to stay before the first drink.

A few facts explain why guessing goes wrong:

- **Only time lowers your BAC, and it takes longer than most people think.** After a heavy night, alcohol can still be in your blood many hours later.
- **Your BAC can keep rising after your last drink.** Alcohol still in your stomach and small intestine continues to be absorbed for a while, often 30 to 90 minutes or more. Leaving "right after the last drink" can mean driving at your peak.
- **Sleep doesn't speed it up.** You can still be over the limit the next morning after a late night of heavy drinking. Morning-after drunk-driving arrests are common for exactly this reason.

Our guide on [how long alcohol stays in your system](/never-hungover/how-long-does-alcohol-stay-in-your-system) explains the timeline in more detail, and [how long it takes for alcohol to kick in](/never-hungover/how-long-does-it-take-for-alcohol-to-kick-in) covers the rising side of the curve.

### Myths that don't lower your BAC

None of these speed up how fast your body clears alcohol:

- **Coffee.** Caffeine can make you feel more alert, but it does nothing to your BAC. A wide-awake drunk driver is still a drunk driver.
- **Cold showers or fresh air.** They might wake you up. They don't lower your blood alcohol.
- **Water.** Staying hydrated is good for you, but drinking water doesn't flush alcohol out faster in any meaningful way.
- **Throwing up.** Alcohol that's already in your blood stays there.
- **Breath mints, gum, or mouthwash.** These may cover the smell, not the alcohol. Some mouthwashes contain alcohol and can briefly push a breath reading higher, not lower.

For more on what does and doesn't affect the clearing rate, see [how to speed up alcohol metabolism](/never-hungover/how-to-speed-up-alcohol-metabolism). And if you're wondering about the smell, [how long alcohol stays on your breath](/never-hungover/how-long-does-alcohol-stay-on-your-breath) explains why it can linger even after your BAC has dropped.

## The Morning After: Hungover Driving

Even once your BAC is back to zero, a bad hangover can affect your driving. Hangovers bring fatigue, poor sleep, headache, slower reactions, and trouble concentrating. Some studies using driving simulators have found that people with a significant hangover drive worse than when they're fully recovered, even with no alcohol left in their system.

Being hungover isn't illegal on its own. But if you feel foggy, exhausted, or slow the morning after a heavy night, it's worth treating that like any other kind of impaired driving: wait, rest, or find another way to get where you're going.

## Penalties: What a DUI Can Cost

Penalties vary a lot by state and by whether it's a first offense, but even a first DUI with no crash and no injuries usually brings some combination of:

- License suspension or revocation
- Fines and court costs, often adding up to thousands of dollars once you include fees, classes, and towing
- Much higher car insurance premiums for several years
- Mandatory alcohol education or treatment programs
- An ignition interlock device (a breath-testing lock on your car) in many states
- Possible jail time, especially for high BAC readings, repeat offenses, or crashes

Many states also have tougher "aggravated" or "extreme" DUI penalties for very high readings, often starting around 0.15% or higher. A DUI conviction can also show up on background checks and affect jobs that involve driving, professional licenses, and travel to some countries.

None of this compares to the real cost, which is hurting or killing yourself or someone else. That's the reason the laws exist.

## A Simple Plan That Beats Counting Drinks

Since you can't reliably know your BAC, the practical answer is to make the decision before you start drinking.

- **Decide how you're getting home first.** Pick a designated driver who isn't drinking at all, book a ride, or plan to stay over.
- **If you're the driver, don't drink.** Not "just one," not "I'll wait an hour." Zero is the only number that removes the guesswork.
- **Keep rideshare or taxi apps ready.** The cost of a ride is small next to the cost of a DUI.
- **Watch out for friends.** If someone who has been drinking is about to drive, offer a ride, call them a car, or take their keys if you can do so safely.
- **Plan for the morning too.** After a late, heavy night, assume you might still be over the limit when you wake up.

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

Since this is a site about DHM (dihydromyricetin), let's be completely clear: **DHM does not lower your blood alcohol level in any way that matters for driving.** There is no good evidence that DHM, or any other supplement, can make you legal or safe to drive after drinking. Nothing you take changes the advice above.

What some people use DHM for is the next day. DHM is a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and hangover symptoms. Most of the research comes from animal and lab studies, with limited human data, so it's best viewed as promising rather than proven. People who drink socially and want to feel better the morning after sometimes take it alongside sensible habits like eating, pacing their drinks, and staying hydrated.

If you want to try it, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when. Just remember that a supplement is about how you feel tomorrow, not whether you can drive tonight.

## The Bottom Line

- The US legal limit is **0.08% BAC** for adult drivers, **0.05% in Utah**, **0.04% for commercial drivers**, and **0.00% to 0.02% for drivers under 21**.
- Many other countries set the limit at **0.05%** or lower, and some at or near zero.
- You can be charged with impaired driving **below the legal limit**, and driving skills decline from around 0.02%.
- There's no reliable way to count drinks and know you're under the limit. Body size, sex, food, and drink strength all change the result.
- Your body clears alcohol at roughly one standard drink per hour, and nothing (coffee, water, cold showers) speeds that up.
- The safest plan is the simplest: if you're driving, don't drink. If you've been drinking, don't drive.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What is the legal blood alcohol limit to drive in the US?**

For drivers 21 and older, the legal limit is 0.08% BAC in every state except Utah, where it's 0.05%. Commercial drivers have a 0.04% limit, and drivers under 21 face zero tolerance limits of 0.00% to 0.02%, depending on the state. You can also be charged with impaired driving below these limits if alcohol has affected how you drive.

**How many drinks does it take to reach 0.08%?**

There's no reliable number. Body weight, sex, food, how fast you drink, and the actual size and strength of your drinks all change the result, sometimes a lot, so any chart is only a rough average that may not fit you on a given night. A single large craft beer or a strong pour can count as two or more standard drinks.

**Can you get a DUI if you're under 0.08%?**

Yes. Most states let police charge you with impaired driving if alcohol has affected your ability to drive safely, even if your BAC is below the legal limit. Evidence can include your driving, your behavior, and field sobriety tests. Drivers under 21 and commercial drivers also face lower limits.

**What is the legal driving limit in Canada, the UK, and Australia?**

In Canada, driving at 0.08% or above is a criminal offense, and most provinces apply roadside license suspensions from 0.05%. England and Wales use 0.08%, while Scotland uses 0.05%. Australia uses 0.05% nationwide, with zero tolerance for learner and probationary drivers. Laws change, so check local rules before driving abroad.

**How long after drinking can I legally drive?**

There is no reliable way to work out the moment you become legal again. Only time lowers your BAC, the rate varies from person to person, your BAC can keep rising for a while after your last drink, and you can still be over the limit the next morning. When in doubt, don't drive. Arrange a ride or a place to stay before you start drinking.

**Does coffee or water lower your blood alcohol level?**

No. Coffee may make you feel more awake, and water helps with hydration, but neither speeds up how fast your liver clears alcohol. The same goes for cold showers, fresh air, and eating after you've finished drinking. Only time lowers your BAC.

**Why is Utah's limit 0.05%?**

Utah lowered its limit from 0.08% to 0.05%, with the change taking effect at the end of 2018, to reduce alcohol-related crashes. Driving skills such as coordination, tracking moving objects, and reacting to emergencies are already reduced at around 0.05%, and many countries in Europe and elsewhere use the same limit.

**Can DHM lower your BAC so you can drive?**

No. There is no good evidence that DHM or any other supplement lowers your blood alcohol enough to make driving legal or safe. Some people take DHM to help with how they feel the next day, but it has no place in deciding whether to drive. If you've been drinking, don't drive.
